If any declarations, covenants and restrictions are associated with any land in the subdivision, no Zoning Permit will be issued until all declarations, covenants and restrictions have been executed and filed with the Lincoln County Registry of Deeds, and a copy provided to the Office of the Code Enforcement Officer.
To provide a development review process that applies to a conceptual plan coordinating the development of blocks, roads, civic space, and other neighborhood level design.
To show mandatory compliance standards for blocks, shopfront streets, alleys, roads, district mix, and building mix, as applicable.
To allow an applicant to gain conceptual-level approval for a project without preparing detailed site plans or architectural and engineering drawings for roads, civic spaces, lots, or buildings.
To authorize the Code Enforcement Office to accept applications for subsequent development review in accordance with this Code, as project phases and individual lots are built out.
Parcels under single ownership that involve the potential for significant or phased development.
Any proposed reassignment of districts to land on the District Map.
The Planning Board reviews and approves all applications for master plan approval.
The review and approval of an application for Master Plan application is conducted at a public hearing.
Within 30 days of receiving an application for Master Plan approval, the Planning Board must review the application for completeness and hold a public hearing.
The Planning Board shall forward Master Plan applications for Life Safety review, in accordance with Article 7.29 Life Safety.
Within 30 days of the closing of the public hearing, the Planning Board must make a decision to approve, approve with conditions, deny, or grant withdrawal of the application.
When considering a revision to a previously approved application for Master Plan approval, the Planning Board must limit its review to the proposed changes to the previously approved application.
Plans for project phases under a Master Plan may be submitted as Large Project Plans, Small Project plans, or Subdivision Plans, as appropriate.
For Master Plans that involve realignment of districts, see Article 7 Section C.2 Zoning Amendment.
The Planning Board must approve a Master Plan application and issue findings of fact upon verifying consistency to the following:
The purpose and purpose of this Code.
The purpose of the District(s) where the property is located.
The adopted Comprehensive Plan of the Town of Newcastle.
Considerations indicated elsewhere in this Code for the required Master Plan approval.
The Planning Board may require the posting of a bond or other performance guarantee to assure compliance with the Master Plan and/or conditions, as approved.
The Planning Board may attach conditions and/or limitations that it deems necessary in order to ensure compliance to the standards applicable to development requiring Master Plan approval.
To request to make changes to a previously approved application for development review.
Plan amendments that are not de minimis in nature are subject to review by the Code Enforcement Officer.

The Code Enforcement Officer must determine whether a plan revision is de minimis in nature and thereupon review said revision administratively or determine if the Permitting Authority should review the petition based on the nature of the request and initial plan approval.
In accordance with Article 7.B.4.F Amendments and Modifications, the Code Enforcement Officer may determine whether a Subdivision Plan revision is de minimis or requires action by the Planning Board.

Within 14 days after receiving a completed application for a plan revision, the Code Enforcement Officer must review the application and determine if the proposed revision is de minimis or significant enough to be considered a major amendment to the plan.
The Code Enforcement Officer may determine the proposed revision is de minimis upon finding that the revised plan:
Does not contravene the previously published public notice, any finding, or attached condition made by the Permitting Authority for the original application;
Does not detrimentally impact matters of substance identified in the meeting minutes of the original public meetings or public hearings;
Insignificant changes to the original application that do not constitute a substantial change in operational or built outcome, in that persons familiar with the plan would not notice the change.
Upon a determination that the proposed revision is de minimis, the Code Enforcement Officer will approve or deny the proposed revision in writing.

Upon a determination that the proposed revision is not de minimis, the Code Enforcement Officer must notify, in writing, the applicant and the designated Permitting Authority of the determination and the applicant must submit the proposed revisions to the designated Permitting Authority as a revision to a previously approved plan in accordance with this Code.
When considering a revision to a previously approved plan, the review must be limited to the proposed changes to the previously approved plan.

Where an approved revision causes need for a new plan mylar to be signed by the Planning Board and recorded at the Lincoln County Registry of Deeds, the Planning Board must make itself available as a board or as individuals to sign mylars within 14 days. After obtaining signatures, the applicant must file said mylars in accordance with the standards of this Code.
To authorize a Use on a parcel of land, in a building or group of buildings, in accordance with the list of permittable Uses located in the Use Table for each District.
Applies to all applications seeking to engage in a new Use or a change of Use on a parcel of land, in a building, or group of buildings.
The permitting authority for Use Permits are desginated on each District page.

Within 30 days of receiving a completed application for a Use Permit, the designated permitting authority shall review the application and approve, approve with modifications, deny, or grant withdrawal of the application and file the decision with the Town Clerk.
The permitting authority may, at their discretion, solicit comment from or move that the application be reviewed for approval by another permitting authority.
This action may extend the application review deadline by an additional 30 days.

Referal to a permitting authority such as a State, Federal, or another agency not under the jurisdiction of the municipality shall not have a review deadline. However, the municipality shall exercise due dilligence to ensure applications are reviewed in a timely manner.
No Use Permit application may be approved by a permitting authority that does not have the legal means to do so under the authority granted by this Code, or by State or Federal law.
To authorize a Use in a lower density District under circumstances that would otherwise only be permittable in a District with higher density.
Applies to all applications seeking to engage in a new Expanded Use or a change of Use either to or from an Expanded Use.
Expanded Use Permit Authority and Proceedure follow those of Article 7 Section 15.C and 15.D respectively.

To authorize a Use on a parcel of land, in a building or group of buildings in accordance with the list of permittable Uses located in the Use Table for each District, and which Use is symbiotic with a dwelling use.
Applies to all applications seeking to engage in a new Residential Companion Use or a change of Use either to or from a Residential Companion Use.
Residential Companion Use Permit Authority and Proceedure follow those of Article 7 Section 15.C and 15.D respectively.
To authorize a predetermined type of exception from the standards in this Code, within specific limitations and subject to performance measures.
Special permits may only be requested as specifically authorized by this Code.

No Zoning Permit must be issued for development that requires or requests a special permit until the discretionary review process for a special permit has been completed in accordance with the standards of this Article.
The approval or denial of an application for a special permit is in the reasonable discretion of the Planning Board.
The Planning Board reviews and decides all applications that require a Special Permit.
The granting of a special permit authorizes the Code Enforcement Officer to issue a Zoning Permit.
Within 30 days after receiving a completed application for development review that requires a special permit, the Planning Board must review the application and hold a public hearing.

Within 45 days after closing of the public hearing, the Planning Board must make a decision to approve, approve with modifications, deny, or grant withdrawal the application for a special permit, and file said decision with the Town Clerk.
When considering a revision to a previously approved application for a special permit, the Planning Board must limit its review to the proposed changes to the previously approved application.
When determining whether to approve or deny an application, the Planning Board must consider the following:
The adopted Comprehensive Plan of the Town of Newcastle;
The purpose and intent of this Code;
The purpose of the District(s) where the property is located;

The proposed use or activity will be established, maintained, and operated so as to be harmonious with the surrounding area and will not impede the development, use, and quiet enjoyment of abutting property in any foreseeable manner;

The proposed use or activity will be of a character that does not produce excessive noise, heat, glare, dust, smoke, fumes, odors, or vibration detectable off the property or that adversely affects the surrounding area;
The proposed use or activity will not result in the destruction, loss, or damage of any feature determined to be of significant natural, scenic or historic importance; and,
Considerations indicated elsewhere in this Code for special permit approval.

In granting a special permit, the Planning Board may attach conditions and/or limitations that it deems necessary in order to ensure compliance to the findings and/or standards for the specific special permit requested. Such conditions may include, but are not limited to, buffers, screening, limits on location, scale, intensity, design, lighting, signs and hours of operation.

Failure to comply with any condition or restriction constitutes a violation of this Code and, in addition to any civil or criminal remedy or enforcement procedure, is grounds for modification, suspension, or revocation of the special permit.

Special permit approvals must be acted upon within 2 years from the date the decision is filed with the Town Clerk, excluding any time required awaiting the decision of an appeal. If a special permit is not acted upon with 2 years, the approval expires.
The Planning Board may reduce the time period that a special permit remains valid to a shorter time period as a condition attached to the special permit.

The Planning Board may extend the duration of validity for a special permit upon making a finding that a demonstrated hardship has prevented utilization of the rights authorized by the special permit.

Requests for extension of the duration of validity must be submitted to the Office of the Code Enforcement Officer in a timely manner so as to be scheduled and heard by the Planning Board prior to expiration of the special permit.
To allow a deviation from certain dimensional standards in this Code only when strict application of the Ordinance to the applicant or applicant’s property would cause undue hardship.
In accordance with Title 30-A SS.4353(4), an Undue Hardship Variance may not be granted for uses.

In accordance with Title 30-A SS.4353(4-C), a Practical Difficulty variance of the following dimensional standards may be granted: lot area, lot coverage, frontage, and setback requirements, and may not be granted for uses.

In accordance with Title 30-A SS.4353.4-a Disability Variance, a variance may be granted for the installation of equipment or construction of structures necessary for access to or egress from a dwelling by a person with a disability, or the construction of non-commercial vehicle storage.
No Zoning Permit may be issued for development that requests a variance until the review process for a variance has been completed in accordance with the standards of this Article.
The Board of Appeals reviews and decides all applications for a zoning variance.
Within 30 days after receiving a completed application for a Zoning Permit that requires a variance, the Board of Appeals must review the application and hold a public hearing.

Within 45 days of the closing of the public hearing, the Board of Appeals must make a decision to approve, approve with conditions, deny, or grant withdrawal of the application for a variance and issue a certificate to the applicant stating the following:
Current property owner and identifying the property by reference to the last recorded deed in its chain of title.
What the variance has been granted for, including any conditions on the variance.
Date of decision.
Within 90 days of issuance of a certificate, the applicant must file a copy of the decision with the Lincoln County Registry of Deeds.
The granting of a variance is based upon demonstrated need, not convenience, and when no other feasible alternative is available.
In addition to the Disability Variance in Title 30-A SS.4353.4-a, the Board of Appeals may only grant two types of Variance:
Undue Hardship Variance; and
Practical Difficulty Variance.
The Board may grant an Undue Hardship Variance when it finds that all of the following conditions exist:
The land in question cannot yield a reasonable return unless a variance is granted;
The need for a variance is due to the unique circumstances of the property and not to the general conditions in the neighborhood;
The granting of a variance will not alter the essential character of the locality; and
The hardship is not the result of action taken by the applicant or a prior owner.
The Board may grant a Practical Difficulty Variance when it finds that all of the following conditions exist:
The need for a variance is due to the unique circumstances of the property and not to the general condition of the neighborhood;
The granting of a variance will not produce an undesirable change in the character of the neighborhood and will not unreasonably detrimentally affect the use or market value of abutting properties;
The practical difficulty is not the result of action taken by the petitioner or a prior owner;
No other feasible alternative to a variance is available to the petitioner;
The granting of a variance will not unreasonably adversely affect the natural environment;
The property is not located in whole or in part within shoreland areas as described in Title 38, Section 435.; and,

Desirable relief could be granted without causing substantial detriment to the public good and without nullifying or substantially derogating from the purpose and purpose of a specific district in this Code or the Ordinance in general.
The Board of Appeals may attach conditions and/ or limitations it deems necessary in order to ensure compliance to the findings and/or standards for the specific variance requested.

Failure to comply with any condition or restriction constitutes a violation of this Code and, in addition to any civil or criminal remedy or enforcement procedure, is grounds for modification, suspension, or revocation of the variance.
Projects benefiting from a variance must be completed within two years of the granting of the variance.
For projects not completed within two years, the variance will be revoked.
Upon written request by an applicant, the Board of Appeals may, in its discretion, extend the time period that a variance remains valid for up to 6 months.

Requests for extension of the duration of validity must be submitted to the Office of the Code Enforcement Officer in a timely manner so as to be scheduled and heard by the Board of Appeals prior to expiration of the special permit.
To request the Town to accept a voluntary offering of a building, road, property easement, or civic space for public dedication.
Any project that contains a building, road, property easement, or civic space.

The Board of Selectmen review all land conveyance petitions on behalf of the Town. The Board of Selectmen may elect to place a land conveyance petition on the warrant of an Annual or Special Town Meeting, where by acceptance would be determined by a majority vote at Town Meeting.
The approval or denial of a land conveyance petition is a discretionary legislative act, subject to a majority vote of the Board of Selectmen.

Within 60 days after receiving a land conveyance petition, the Board of Selectmen must review the petition at a regular scheduled meeting, and take action to accept the conveyance, deny the conveyance, or place it on the warrant of the next occurring Town Meeting.
The Board of Selectmen may elect to hold a public hearing.
The Board of Selectmen may decide to consult the Code Enforcement Officer or the Planning Board prior to taking action.
A majority vote of the Board of Selectmen is required to accept a voluntary offering of land for public dedication.
In developing its recommendation to the Board of Selectmen, the Code Enforcement Officer or Planning Board may consider the following:
The adopted Comprehensive Plan of the Town of Newcastle.
The purpose of the District where the property is located.
Any demonstrated public interest in ownership and the assumption of maintenance responsibility for the land in question.

The Code Enforcement Officer or Planning Board may make recommendations to the Board of Selectmen when it deems that accepting a petition to convey land to the Town of Newcastle is within the public interest.
To provide an applicant a way to change zoning regulations in response to changes in Newcastle policy or factors or conditions that may be affecting real property.
Any project within the Town of Newcastle.
The Board of Selectmen process all requests for zoning text or map amendments and place requests for amendments on the Annual or Special Town Meeting.
The approval or denial of a zoning text or map amendment is a discretionary legislative act, by majority vote at an Annual or Special Town Meeting.
Petitions may be submitted by any of the following:
Any member(s) of the Board of Selectmen.
The Code Enforcement Officer.
The Board of Appeals.
The Planning Board.
A property owner seeking to change the entitlement of his/her own property.
10% of the number of voters who voted in the Town of Newcastle in the last gubernatorial election.

Within 14 days of receiving a petition to amend the zoning text or map, the Board of Selectmen must submit the petition and the proposed changes, additions, or repeal of language to the Planning Board for review.

Within 30 days after receiving a petition to amend the zoning text or map, the Planning Board must review the petition and accompanying documentation at a regular meeting of the Planning Board. The Planning Board will consider the petition and must provide a written recommendation to the Board of Selectmen, considering the following:
The adopted Comprehensive Plan of the Town of Newcastle.
The purpose of this Code, in general.
The purpose of the district(s) that would be applied to the properties in question.

Within 45 days after submittal to the Board of Selectmen, the Board of Selectmen must review the petition and any recommendations of the Planning Board, hold a public hearing, and vote to place it on the warrant of the next occurring Town Meeting or Special Town Meeting.
To protect significant historic structures and sites from demolition, neglect, or disturbance;
To facilitate the relocation or salvage of historic structures deemed ineligible for National Register nomination, as an alternative to demolition;
To facilitate the permanent protection of a historic structure or site by providing an opportunity for third- party acquisition of the site;
To facilitate the archaeological recovery of any historic artifacts; and,
To provide an opportunity for documentation of historic structures ineligible for National Register nomination, where demolition, salvage or relocation is intended.
The provisions of this Code apply to all structures existing on or before 1900 and sites with known or suspect historic or pre-historic settlement pre-dating 1900.
The Code Enforcement Officer shall review and approve all demolition permits, and consult with the Newcastle Historical Society or equal party as needed.
Demolition of Historic Structure:

An historic structure may not be demolished for a period no less than 90 days from the time that an applicant sends a letter to request determination by Maine Historic Preservation Commission whether a structure is eligible for the National Register of Historic Places or is a contributing structure to an eligible Historic District. The 90 day delay period commences on the date proof of mailing to Maine Historic Preservation Commission is provided to the Office of the Code Enforcement Officer.

An applicant shall obtain a letter from Maine Historic Preservation Commission or from a qualified historic preservation consultant as to whether the structure is ELIGIBLE for the National Register of Historic Places or as a contributing structure to an eligible Historic District. (To be “eligible” is only an opinion; it is not an application process.);

If the structure is estimated to be eligible, no demolition is permitted. If the owner wishes to formally apply to the Register and his property is declined, the status of the property shall be reconsidered;

Any structure existing on or before 1900 that is not considered eligible for the National Register shall be advertised by the owner as available for free, offering to the general public the structure to be moved or scrapped for salvage materials at his/her expense. The advertisement shall appear in a newspaper of local circulation, a minimum of two times per month, for a period no less than 90 days. Any other interested party may advertise the building during those 90 days; and,

During the 90 day time period, the Newcastle Historical Society or equal party shall be permitted by the owner to document the structure inside and out prior to the structure’s relocation or destruction.
Demolition of Historic Structure Due to Neglect: At any time, any party may raise concerns of historic structural neglect to the Code Enforcement Officer.

Staff may investigate concerns of historic structural neglect and issue a notice of violation to a property owner who allows a structure to suffer structural failure as a result of exposure, and issue fines; and,

Alternatively, the Town may make minimal repairs to the structure to prevent it from deteriorating further and bill the owner for the incurred costs. Any unpaid fines or repair will be placed in lien against the property.
Demolition or Disturbance of Historic Archaeological Resources:

An applicant shall obtain a letter from Maine Historic Preservation Commission or from a qualified historic archaeologist as to whether the site may contain historic archaeological resources and is ELIGIBLE for the National Register of Historic Places or as a contributing site to a Historic District. (To be “eligible” is only an opinion; it is not an application process);

If the site is estimated to be eligible, no demolition or disturbance is permitted. If the owner wishes to formally apply to the Register and his/her property is declined, the status of the property shall be reconsidered;

If the site is estimated not to be eligible, the town may withhold issuing a demolition permit for a period of 90 days, during which time the Newcastle Historical Society or equal party shall be permitted by the owner to document the site and perform archaeological test digs; and,

If significant artifacts are discovered, the Newcastle Historical Society or equal party may petition the Town of Newcastle to extend demolition for a period of up to 1 year to facilitate recovery and documentation of artifacts.

To provide an applicant a way to petition the Town to rectify a failure to act, denial of a permit, decision made, or enforcement action taken by the Code Enforcement Officer or Planning Board when an alleged error or misinterpretation has been made in the enforcement or application of the standards of this Code.
Any aggrieved party may appeal an interpretation, order, requirement, direction, or failure to act by a Code Enforcement Officer within 30 days of such action or failure to act.
An appeal of a Variance constitutes a judicial appeal.
An appeal of written interpretations, development plans, special permits, plan revisions constitute an administrative appeal.
The Board of Appeals holds a “de novo” hearing to review and decide appeals of decisions of the Code Enforcement Officer as applicable in this Code.
The Board of Appeals holds an appellate hearing to review and decides appeals of decisions of the Planning Board as applicable in this Code.
Within 30 days of an action or failure to act, any aggrieved party may file an appeal with the Appellate Authority.
Within 30 days of receiving an appeal, the Appellate Authority must review the application and hold a public hearing.

Within 45 days after the closing of the public hearing, the Appellate Authority must make a decision to uphold or reverse the decision of the Code Enforcement Officer, and file said decision with the Town Clerk.
In accordance with MRSA Title 30 Section 2691, an applicant may file a request to the Board of Appeals to reconsider its decision within 10 days of the decision.
The Board of Appeals will hold a public hearing, and vote to reconsider its decision.

If a majority of Board members who originally voted on the decision vote to reconsider, the Board of Appeals may conduct additional hearings, and receive additional evidence and testimony before taking action.
If the Board of Appeals reconsiders its original decision, the Board must conclude its deliberations and vote within 45 days of the original decision.
Decisions of the Planning Board may not be reconsidered.

To provide an applicant a way to petition the Town to rectify the failure to act, denial of a permit, decision made, or enforcement action taken by a Code Enforcement Officer or the Planning Board when an alleged error or misinterpretation has been made in the enforcement or application of the standards of this Code.
Any aggrieved party may appeal a decision or action of the Board of Appeals to the Maine Superior Court.
An appeal of a Variance constitutes a judicial appeal.
An aggrieved party may file an appeal at the Maine Superior Court pursuant to the Maine Rules of Civil Procedure.

To provide for the continuation of uses, structures, building lots, site characteristics, or signs that were established prior to the adoption of this Code and were made nonconforming in result of the adoption of this Code.
To provide clear and fair rules for when nonconforming conditions should come into conformance with the standards contained within this Code.
All building lots, uses, buildings, components, roofs, site characteristics, signs, roads or other items that were established prior to the adoption of this Code.

Nonconforming conditions may continue to operate until such a time as the owner of the property, building, or features makes an alteration that requires conformity, as described in related sections of this Code.
The applicant has the burden of establishing the existence of a nonconforming condition that was in effect prior to the adoption of this Code.

When applying for any permit or approval related to a nonconforming condition, the applicant may be required to submit evidence of a prior permit or other documentation showing that the nonconformity existed prior to the adoption of this Code.
The Code Enforcement Officer will determine all questions as to whether a nonconforming condition exists, and prepare a written interpretation in accordance with Article 7.A.6 Written Interpretation.

The written interpretation must assign a building type, components, roof type, and any other features to the nonconforming building, to set the baseline for modifications that can be legally made to the nonconforming building.
A Zoning Permit is required for the rebuilding, restoration, repair, or reconstruction of a nonconforming condition within one year of the date of damage or destruction.
The Code Enforcement Officer may grant a one-year extension of this period.

In the event that a Zoning Permit is not obtained within one year of the date of damage or destruction, and no extension is requested, then the nonconforming condition may not be reestablished unless it conforms to all regulations of this Code.
The Code Enforcement Officer is appointed by the Board of Selectmen.
The Code Enforcement Officer is the enforcement authority for this Code. The Code Enforcement Officer may seek the advice of the Development Administrator on an as needed basis.

The Code Enforcement Officer may issue any enforcement order, violation notice, request for compliance, or other correspondence as necessary and institute any appropriate inspection, action, or proceeding in the name of the Town of Newcastle to:
Prevent the unlawful erection, relocation, extension, enlargement, or alteration of any structure or sign;
Prevent the unlawful use or occupancy of real property;
Prevent any illegal act, business, or use in or about any premises; and
Prevent, correct, restrain, or abate violations of this Code.
The Code Enforcement Officer establishes application forms and requirements for application review in collaboration with the Development Administrator.
The Code Enforcement Officer reviews and approves applications for:
Small Project Plan
Large Project Plan
De minimis changes to previously approved plans
The Code Enforcement Officer may grant waivers of standards as explicitly permitted by this Code.
The Code Enforcement Officer prepares recommendations for Master Plan and Special Permit and Subdivision applications reviewed by the Planning Board.
The Code Enforcement Officer performs site inspections as needed.
The Code Enforcement Officer, from time to time, provides written reports and recommendations to other Permitting Authorities and to the Board of Selectmen.
The Code Enforcement Officer must not issue any written interpretation or Zoning Permit in violation of this Code.
Any written interpretation or Zoning Permit may be revoked upon finding any material misstatement of fact or misrepresentation in plans or specifications by the applicant.

The Code Enforcement Officer, upon finding evidence of violation of this Code will give written notice to the property owner and/or occupant of said property demanding such violation be corrected or abated within such time as the Code Enforcement Officer deems appropriate.
Nothing in this Code will restrict the Town from seeking immediate equitable relief for a violation of this Code from a court of competent jurisdiction without prior notice.

Any person who violates the standards of this Code will be fined in accordance to a schedule of fines established by the Board of Selectmen and posted in the Town Office or pursuant to the terms of Title 30-A Section 4452.
The Planning Board must consist of a minimum 5 members, all legal residents of the Town of Newcastle, appointed by the Board of Selectmen to serve staggered terms of 3 years.
The Planning Board reviews and approves all applications for:
Master Plan
Subdivision Plan
Special Permit
The Planning Board may grant waivers of standards as explicitly permitted by this Code.
The Planning Board reviews and approves applications in accordance with the following ordinances
Shoreland
Wind
Towers
Sediment and Erosion Control
Mobile Home Parks
The Planning Board provides advice and recommendations to the Board of Selectmen concerning the following:
Proposed amendments to zoning text or maps of this Code.
The laying out, alteration, relocation, or discontinuance of public ways and statutory private ways.
The proposed conveyance of land to the Town.
The Planning Board, or its designee, is responsible for the authoring and periodical update of the Comprehensive Plan for the Town of Newcastle, and its subsequent adoption.
The Planning Board, or its designee, drafts the official map of the Town of Newcastle.
The Planning Board may adopt rules of procedure and policy as it may deem necessary to conduct its affairs, including but not limited to the following subjects:
Rules and procedures governing applications, including required written and graphical information;
Rules and procedures pertaining to the development review process;
Rules and procedures governing the administrative compliance of zoning requirements;
Rules and procedures for subdivision
The adoption or amendment of rules of procedure and policy is conducted administratively at a public meeting.
The Board of Appeals will consist of 5 members, all legal residents of the Town of Newcastle, appointed by the Board of Selectmen to serve staggering terms of 3 years.
The Board of Selectmen may appoint alternate members as deemed appropriate, which members may vote in the absence of a regular member.
The Board of Appeals reviews and decides:
Applications for a Variance; and,
Administrative Appeals of decisions of the Code Enforcement Officer and the Planning Board.
Administrative Appeals of decisions of the Code Enforcement Officer and the Planning Board for waivers of standards as explicitly permitted by this Code.
The Board of Appeals may adopt rules of procedure and policy as it may deem necessary to conduct its affairs, including but not limited to the following subjects:
Rules and procedures governing applications, including required written and graphical information; and,
Rules and procedures governing the administrative compliance of zoning requirements.
The adoption or amendment of rules of procedure and policy is conducted administratively at a public meeting.

To provide for Life Safety review of projects including the development of individual buildings or groups of buildings, modifications to buildings, or changes or alterations made to a site where Life Safety considerations and standards apply.
Life Safety review shall be applicable as follows:
Any Small Project Plan permit application that includes the following;
Single Unit Commercial Buildings
Multi-unit Commercial Buildings
Mixed-use Buildings
Multi-unit Residential Buildings
Commercial Accessory Buildings
All Large Project Plan permit applications.
All Subdivision permit applications.
All Master Plan permit applications.

The Newcastle Board of Selectmen shall appoint a Life Safety Officer, or the Newcastle Fire Chief as the Life Safety Officer, for the purposes of Life Safety review in compliance with this Code, the NFPA 101 Life Safety Code, and other applicable Municipal, State, or Federal laws or standards.
The Code Enforcement Officer shall forward applicable permit applications to the Life Safety Officer for review, and;
Consult with the Life Safety Officer on Small Project Plan permit applications.
Obtain a written Life Safety review report from the Life Safety Officer on the following permit applications;
Large Project Plan
Subdivision Plan
Master Plan

The Life Safety Officer shall reference the NFPA 101 Life Safety Code, and other applicable Municipal State or Federal laws and standards, in reviewing permit applications, and where appropriate provide references to specific standards when providing a written report to the Code Enforcement Officer.

children.heading: Abandoned
children.text: When a building, commercial unit, or property becomes vacant and unoccupied for a period of one year or more is deemed abandoned.

children.heading: Absolute Height
children.text: Height is measured from the surface of the ground to the highest point on a building, component, sign, or other structure.

children.heading: Abutting
children.text: Having any segment of a real property boundary in common, or separated by a right-of-way, alley, or easement.

children.heading: Abutter
children.text: An owner of property located within a certain distance of a subject property considered for development.

children.heading: Access
children.text: The way or means to enter and leave property or structure.

children.heading: Accessory Building
children.text: See Building, Accessory.

children.heading: Accessory Dwelling Unit
children.text: An additional permitted dwelling unit located in a component of a primary building or in an accessory building.

children.heading: Accessory Unit
children.text: An additional permitted residential or commercial unit located in a component of a primary building or in an accessory building.

children.heading: Additional Structure
children.text: Any item constructed or erected, not including a primary or accessory buildings, the use of which requires more or less permanent location on the ground, or attached to something having permanent location on the ground.

children.heading: Adjacent
children.text: To be located in close proximity, or the closest instance of a referenced element, but not directly touching.

children.heading: Affordable Housing Development
children.text: A development in which 51% or more of the dwelling units are deed restricted to meet the definition of Affordable Housing, Owned or Affordable Housing, Rental.

children.heading: Affordable Housing, Owned
children.text: An owner-occupied dwelling unit for which the occupying household’s income does not exceed 120% of the median income for the area as defined by the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development under the United States Housing Act of 1937, Public Law 75-412, 50 Stat. 888, Section 8, as amended, and said household can afford the unit without spending more than 30% of the household’s monthly income on housing costs.

children.heading: Affordable Housing, Rental
children.text: A dwelling unit which a household whose income does not exceed 80% of the median income for the area as defined by the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development under the United States Housing Act of 1937, Public Law 75-412, 50 Stat. 888, Section 8, as amended, can afford the unit without spending more than 30% of the household’s monthly income on housing costs.

children.heading: Agent
children.text: A person who acts on behalf of another person or group.

children.heading: Agricultural Buildings
children.text: Buildings associated with the planting, cultivating, producing, growing, and harvesting of agricultural or horticultural products, the raising of livestock and poultry, and any work performed in conjunction with the above farm operations, including the packing, drying, and storing of products produced on-premises. Includes buildings for equine, or horse-related activities, including boarding, lessons, rides, breeding, veterinary care, races, events, and shows.

children.heading: Agricultural Building
children.text: Includes storage sheds, apiaries, hoop houses, chicken coops, cold frames, compost bin, greenhouses, silos, rain barrels.

children.heading: Agricultural Use
children.text: The commercial planting, cultivating, producing, growing, and harvesting of agricultural or horticultural products, the raising of livestock and poultry, and any work performed in conjunction with the above farm operations, including the packing, drying, and storing of products produced on-premises. Agriculture also includes all equine, or horse-related activities, including boarding, lessons, rides, breeding, veterinary care, races, events, and shows. Unless otherwise specified in this Code, the term ‘agriculture’ refers to commercial agriculture.

children.heading: Alley
children.text: A type of road typically located internal to a block that provides access to the side or rear of lots. Alleys typically provide access to service areas, parking, and accessory buildings and may contain utility easements.

children.heading: Alteration
children.text: As applied to a building or structure, a change or rearrangement in the exterior structural parts or in the exit facilities; also an enlargement or addition where new construction is connected to an existing structure, whether by extending on a side or by increasing in height, or the moving from 1 location or position to another.

children.heading: Applicant
children.text: A person or entity who has submitted an application for review under applicable standards of this Code.

children.heading: Assigned
children.text: The process of determining the closest reasonable district, building type, component, roof type, use category or other feature of this Code to a nonconforming condition.

children.heading: Attached
children.text: An object may be said to be attached to another when their outer surfaces are permanently in direct contact, or when they share part of their structural system.

children.heading: Auto-Oriented
children.text: Businesses that relate to vehicular sales and service. All auto- oriented uses, definitions, and standards may be found in Article 4 Use Standards.

children.heading: Average Ground Level
children.text: The mean (average) ground level at the corners of the main body of a building type.

children.heading: Basement
children.text: A story of a building that is, in whole or in part, below the first story.

children.heading: Beam
children.text: A large structural framing member.

children.heading: Blank Wall
children.text: A portion of any facade of a building that does not include windows, doors, columns, pilasters, or other architectural features.

children.heading: Block
children.text: The aggregate land area, including alleys, cross weaves, and footpaths, circumscribed by roads.

children.heading: Bracket
children.text: A visual and/or structural support, typically made of metal or wood, projecting from a building face to bear the weight or visually support a building element.

children.heading: Building
children.text: An assemblage of materials and components that form an enclosure including a roof, windows, doors and solid exterior walls, and designed, built, or occupied as a shelter or enclosure for persons, animals, or property. Not synonymous with Structure.

children.heading: Building, Accessory
children.text: An additional building on a lot that may contain a dwelling, a non- dwelling unit, or a commercial unit.

children.heading: Building, Primary
children.text: A permitted building capable of occupying a lot as the sole structure.

children.heading: Building Element
children.text: Any part of a building, including the main building mass, components, and accessory buildings.

children.heading: Building Face
children.text: Any exterior wall of a Building.

children.heading: Building Height
children.text: The measurement of building height by stories, where each full story above average ground level is counted as 1 story. For buildings with a pitched roofs, habitable space is allowed within the pitch and is not considered a full story.

children.heading: Building Mass
children.text: See Main Building Mass.

children.heading: Building Type
children.text: A classification or kind of structure characterized and differentiated by its massing, composition, use, features, and placement on a lot.

children.heading: Caliper
children.text: A measurement of the diameter of a tree trunk. For trees less than 4 inches in diameter, caliper is measured 6 inches from the ground. For trees between 4 inches and 12 inches in diameter, caliper is measured 12 inches from the ground.

children.heading: Carport
children.text: A roofed structure covered on 2 or more sides with fabric, vinyl, plastic, or other similar sheeting material that provides protection from the elements for vehicles or other items.

children.heading: Change of Use
children.text: The act of changing the categorization of activity within a building, structure, or portion thereof from one primary use to another.

children.heading: Chine
children.text: The break-point or horizontal plane formed where two differently sloped portions of a complex roof system meet.

children.heading: Civic Space
children.text: An outdoor open space designed to support social and recreational activities.

children.heading: Civic District
children.text: An area protected from development and designated for use as civic space on the District Map.

children.heading: Core District
children.text: An area that shares common characteristics with other land in the same zoning designation, or is an area that is intended to transition toward a character that has been determined by the community. Core Districts span a range of development intensity from most rural, D1, to most urban, D6.

children.heading: Civic Use
children.text: Activities, uses, purposes, and organizations which are dedicated to arts, culture, education, religion, recreation, government, transit, municipal parking, gardening, horticulture, public gathering, assembly, or meeting. All civic and institutional uses must serve and be open to the public and operate as a non-profit or otherwise be tax exempt. All civic and institutional uses, definitions, and standards may be found in Article 4 Use Standards.

children.heading: Clear Height
children.text: The vertical distance between the underside of an overhanging building element and the horizontal surface below, free from obstruction.

children.heading: Commercial
children.text: Any retail, service, or auto-oriented use that deals with transactions with the public either directly or through remote communication.

children.heading: Commercial Accessory Building
children.text: A building that supports or compliments a commercial use, not a residential use.

children.heading: Component
children.text: One of the elements that make up a building, the other being the main building mass. Components are comprised of smaller attachments to the main building mass and provide architectural articulation and additional usable space.

children.heading: Context
children.text: The condition and qualities of the surrounding spaces and structures.

children.heading: Corbel
children.text: Any bracket, especially one of brick or stone, that typically protrudes only slightly from the face of a building.

children.heading: Corner Lot
children.text: A building lot that has frontage on 2 private or public roads, where the roads intersect.

children.heading: Curb
children.text: The edge of the vehicular pavement that may be raised or flush to a swale. It usually directs the flow of water to the drainage system.

children.heading: Curb Radius
children.text: The distance between the edge and center point of a curved section of curbing at the corner of two intersecting roads. This distance is determined by measuring the radius of a circle that approximates the size of the arc formed by the outside face of the curb.

children.heading: Depth
children.text: The perpendicular, horizontal distance from the primary facade of a building into the lot.

children.heading: Detached
children.text: A dwelling that is physically separated from any other structure or structures except accessory buildings.

children.heading: Development
children.text: The construction, reconstruction, alteration, expansion, extension, or relocation of any building or structure; excavation, earth filling, grading, or mining; any use or change in use of any building or structure or land; any change in building type; or, any expansion in the use of land.

children.heading: Development Site
children.text: The land area encompassed in a development proposal irrespective of the number or configuration of lots, land ownership, and/or municipal boundaries.

children.heading: District Map
children.text: The map or set of maps that shows all land areas subject to, or potentially subject to, regulation by this Code and including Core Districts, Special Districts, and any special requirements.

children.heading: Driveway
children.text: A vehicular way providing access from a Public or Private Road to the interior of a lot, including homes, parking lots, or loading docks. Driveways are not subject to construction specifications required for roads.

children.heading: Dwelling Unit
children.text: A single unit providing complete, independent, living facilities containing 1 or more rooms arranged for use by no more than 4 unrelated individuals living together as a single housekeeping unit with cooking, living, sanitary, and sleeping facilities.

children.heading: Dwelling Unit, Accessory
children.text: See Accessory Dwelling Unit.

children.heading: Easement
children.text: A liberty, privilege, or advantage without profit, which a person(s) may have in the lands of another person(s).

children.heading: Eave
children.text: The soffit resulting from the junction of a building wall and an overhanging roof.

children.heading: Element
children.text: See Building Element.

children.heading: Elevation
children.text: The vertical distance between the average ground plane and the top of the finished first floor of a building.

children.heading: Enclose(d)
children.text: To fill in the spaces between structural supports with latticework, walls, windows, or other non-structural wall covering to increase the usability of an outdoor space.

children.heading: Encroach
children.text: To break the plane of a vertical or horizontal regulatory limit with a structural element, so that it extends into a Setback, above a height limit, or over the sidewalk of a public right-of-way.

children.heading: Encroachment
children.text: Any structural element that breaks the plane of a vertical or horizontal regulatory limit, extending into a setback, above a height limit, or the breaking of such limit by a structural element.

children.heading: Entrance (Primary)
children.text: (see ‘Primary Entrance’)

children.heading: Facade
children.text: The exterior wall of a building oriented in whole or in part toward a Public or Private Road, civic space, or on-site civic space (not including alleys).

children.heading: Face
children.text: The surface of a structure or element, especially one that is presented to the view.

children.heading: Farm
children.text: The land, plants, animals, buildings, structures, ponds and machinery used in the commercial production of agricultural products.

children.heading: Field
children.text: An area of undeveloped land primarily covered by grass, including uncultivated meadows and open areas traditionally used for agricultural purposes.

children.heading: First Floor
children.text: The lowest floor of a building that is not considered a basement.

children.heading: First Floor Elevation
children.text: The height from the average ground level to the surface of the first full floor, measured at the primary front facade of the building.

children.heading: Flag Lot
children.text: A building lot that has frontage along a private or public road which is narrower than the minimum permitted lot width or frontage line length for the district in which it is located. The term “Flag Lot” does not refer to the shape of a lot. Lots may take the shape of a flag provided they meet the standards of the district in which it is located.

children.heading: Flat Roof
children.text: see Roof, Flat.

children.heading: Floor Area, Gross
children.text: The sum area of all floors or accessible levels of a building as measured to the perimeter of the exterior faces of the walls with no deduction for corridors, stairs, closets, thickness of walls, columns or other features.

children.heading: Floor Area, Net (Building)
children.text: The sum area of all floors or accessible levels of a building as measured to the perimeter of the exterior faces of the walls, including enclosed porches, but excluding areas used for accessory garage purposes, basement and cellar areas devoted exclusively to storage and mechanical uses accessory to the operation of the building, off-street loading facilities, malls, plazas, elevator shafts, escalators, stairways and stair landings, and those areas used for the storage, operation, or maintenance of mechanical equipment such as air conditioning and heating apparatus.

children.heading: Floor Area, Net (Unit)
children.text: The sum area of all floors or accessible levels of a single unit as measured to the perimiter of the interior faces of the walls, including enclosed porches, but excluding common spaces, shared areas, or areas not exclusivly associated with that single unit.

children.heading: Footprint
children.text: The total gross floor area of a single story of a building, exclud­ ing all unenclosed components of a building.

children.heading: Forecourt
children.text: A landscaped, semi-public area, open to the sky, formed by a recess in a portion of a building facade.

children.heading: Front (noun)
children.text: A condition in which a building is required to be parallel or perpendicular with a frontage line.

children.heading: Front (verb)
children.text: A condition in which a building is required to be parallel or perpendicular with a frontage line.

children.heading: Front Setback
children.text: The distance from the front lot line to the point where any structure may be constructed.

children.heading: Front Setback, Primary
children.text: The setback required along a primary frontage.

children.heading: Front Setback, Secondary
children.text: The setback required along a secondary frontage.

children.heading: Frontage
children.text: The land area that lies between a building and a public or private road, a right-of-way, an easement, a civic space, or a water body.

children.heading: Frontage, Primary
children.text: The primary frontage is the frontage that abuts the primary road or, if there is no road, it is the frontage that abuts a civic space, right-of-way, or easement.

children.heading: Frontage, Secondary
children.text: On corner lots, the frontage that is oriented toward the road that is not the primary road.

children.heading: Frontage Line
children.text: A lot line bordering a public or private road, a right-of-way, an easement, a civic space, or a water body.

children.heading: Frontage Line, Primary
children.text: The property line along the primary Frontage.

children.heading: Frontage Zone
children.text: The Frontage Zone is the Frontage plus an additional Setback from the front facade of the primary building (see standards for individual districts under Article 2 District Standards). The frontage zone applies along both the primary and secondary frontages, but does not apply to alleys. In the case that a lot is undeveloped, the frontage zone is the area between the front lot line of a property and 30 ft into the site.

children.heading: Fully Enclose(d)
children.text: To fill the space between structural supports with walls of windows.

children.heading: Furnishing Zone
children.text: An area of space that allows for the placement of furniture without impeding the 4 ft of clear width required for pedestrian movement.

children.heading: Garage
children.text: An enclosed area integral to a primary building or accessory building that provides space for parking or storage of vehicles. Not synonymous with the parking garage building type.

children.heading: Garage Doors
children.text: Lifting, sliding, or swinging doors that open into an interior space used for vehicular parking, storage, retail sales, fabrication, or other uses.

children.heading: General Accessory Building
children.text: An accessory building that may be occupied by a residential use or a non-residential use.

children.heading: Grade
children.text: The natural finished ground level of land ground level, or the elevation, at any given point.

children.heading: Ground Plane
children.text: The surface of the ground.

children.heading: Gutter
children.text: A channel at the side or in the middle of street, for leading off surface water.

children.heading: Hardscape
children.text: Ground that has been altered with pavers, crushed materials, or compacted earth, with the intention to be used for pedestrian or vehicular travel.

children.heading: Height
children.text: The distance between two points along a vertical plane.

children.heading: Height, Absolute
children.text: See Absolute Height.

children.heading: Improvements
children.text: Any alteration of land, a lot, a building or a structure.

children.heading: Industrial
children.text: The processing or manufacturing of materials, and activities associated with this work. All industrial uses, definitions, and standards may be found in Article 4 Use Standards.

children.heading: Insular Lot
children.text: A building lot that does not have frontage on a private road, a public road, or a waterbody.

children.heading: Intersect
children.text: A condition where one element touches and/or overlaps with another element.

children.heading: Integral
children.text: A condition that refers to one element being located within another.

children.heading: Integrated
children.text: See Integral.

children.heading: Interior Lot
children.text: A building lot that has a frontage along a single private or public road, easement, or right-of-way.

children.heading: Lamp
children.text: The source of illumination in a lighting fixture.

children.heading: Landscaping
children.text: Landscaping includes areas of arranged plant materials.

children.heading: Large Animals
children.text: Large domestic animals including cows, sheep, pigs, and horses raised for home use or for profit.

children.heading: Length
children.text: In a three-dimensional measurement system, length is a horizontal measurement, distinct and longer than width.

children.heading: Light Source
children.text: The lamp and all refractive, reflective, and translucent light transmitting parts of an outdoor light fixture.

children.heading: Loading Dock
children.text: A platform, dedicated to the loading or unloading of trucks.

children.heading: Lodging
children.text: Premises available for daily and weekly renting of bedrooms. All lodging uses, definitions, and standards may be found in Article 4 Use Standards.

children.heading: Lot
children.text: A designated parcel, tract, or area of land established by a deed or plat, or as otherwise permitted by law. Syn: Parcel or Lot of Record.

children.heading: Lot, Building
children.text: A surveyed, bounded, and deeded plot of land that meets the dimensional standards and requirements of this Code for the zoning district in which the plot of land exists, onto which a building or structure may be erected in compliance with this Code.

children.heading: Lot, Virtual
children.text: A potential lot created by virtual lot lines demarcated on a plan to show and determine conformance with this Code, without the act of legal subdivision. Syn: Potential Lot Lines

children.heading: Lot Area
children.text: The total area contained within the boundary lines of a lot, excluding publicly dedicated and accepted rights-of-way.

children.heading: Lot Depth Lot Line
children.text: Lot depth is defined as the perpendicular distance from the front lot line to the rear lot line; or, if the front and rear lot lines are not parallel, the distance from the midpoint of the front lot line to the mid point of the rear lot line. The boundary that legally and geometrically demarcates a lot.

children.heading: Lot Lines, Multiple
children.text: The condition where the boundaries of a lot take an irregular form and more than one front, side, or rear lot line may exist for a single lot.

children.heading: Lot Line, Virtual
children.text: Potential lot lines demarcated on a plan to show and determine conformance with this Code. Virtual lot lines do not require an act of legal subdivision. Syn: Potential Lot Lines

children.heading: Lot Line, Primary Front
children.text: The lot line(s) that abuts the primary road(s).

children.heading: Lot Line, Secondary Front
children.text: The lot line(s) that abuts the secondary road(s).

children.heading: Lot Line, Rear
children.text: Rear lot line(s) are located opposite the front lot line, do not abut a primary or secondary road, and do not intersect with a front lot line. Where side lot lines meet at a point, the rear lot line is that point.

children.heading: Lot Line, Side
children.text: Any lot line(s) that connect, or connect to, front and rear lot lines. A lot may have multiple side lot lines depending on its shape.

children.heading: Lot Width
children.text: The total length of the front lot line or the distance between side lot lines at the maximum front setback, whichever is greater.

children.heading: Lumens
children.text: The amount of light energy generated by a light source.

children.heading: Main Building Mass
children.text: The volume of a primary or accessory building as defined by the dimensional standards for building type and onto which components and roofs may attach.

children.heading: Master Plan
children.text: A development plan and supporting illustrations and documents providing a framework for future development of a site. A Master Plan provides guidance to the applicant and Town regarding applicable permitting and decision making processes.

children.heading: Mechanical Equipment
children.text: Equipment, devices, and accessories used for water supply, drainage, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, including elevator shafts, heating and cooling units, utility cabinets, and other visible structures that are located on or near a building or structure.

children.heading: Multi-unit Commercial Building
children.text: A building occupied by two or more commercial uses and no residential uses.

children.heading: Residential Building
children.text: A building occupied by one or more residential uses and no commercial uses.

children.heading: Mixed Use Building
children.text: A building occupied by a combination of 1 or more commercial uses and 1 or more residential uses.

children.heading: Natural Materials
children.text: Includes wood, metal, brick, stone, or composites from any of the aforementioned materials.

children.heading: Natural Resources
children.text: The processing or manufacturing of materials, and activities associated with this work. All natural resources uses, definitions, and standards may be found in Article 6 Use Standards.

children.heading: Nonconformity Non-dwelling Unit
children.text: An existing use, structure, lot, site characteristics or sign that, at the time of its legal establishment, was in compliance with the zoning regulations, but after the adoption date of this Code has been made wholly or partially nonconforming. A single, internally connected space that comprises a building or a part of a building that can be occupied by any one of the use categories included in Article 6 Use Standards, except for those under the category of Residential.

children.heading: Office
children.text: The transaction of general business, including administrative, professional, and clerical activities, but excluding retail. All office uses, definitions, and standards may be found in Article 4 Use Standards.

children.heading: On-Site Civic Space
children.text: Civic space owned, maintained, and administered by a private entity, provided on the same lot as a building or on a lot associated with a building group, for the purpose of adding publicly accessible amenity space to a development project.

children.heading: Opening
children.text: A void space in between the expanse of two solid structures or piers.

children.heading: Outdoor Display
children.text: The outdoor exhibition or presentation of products and merchandise available for sale.

children.heading: Outdoor Storage
children.text: The storage of merchandise or material in boxes, crates, on pallets or other kinds of shipping containers; and, garden supplies, building supplies, materials, plants, vehicles and other similar equipment, inventory, merchandise, or supplies not normally brought indoors overnight.

children.heading: Parcel
children.text: See Lot.

children.heading: Parking Lot
children.text: An uncovered area used or designed for the off-street parking of 2 or more motor vehicles, excluding a driveway.

children.heading: Patio
children.text: A hard-surfaced, landscaped space constructed at ground level, usually directly adjacent to a building. A patio is constructed with a finished walking surface laid or poured directly on finished grade. A patio has no permanent roof coverings.

children.heading: Permeable
children.text: A condition in which the ground is covered by previous or porous surfaces or materials, such as through soil, mulch, vegetation, and pavers that allow for the movement or passage of water back into the ground.

children.heading: Permitting Authority
children.text: A person or board granted the authority to conduct project review and approval, in accordance with this Code.

children.heading: Pier
children.text: A solid support designed to sustain vertical pressure, such as used in a section of a wall between windows or other adjacent openings or as structural members used in the construction of building foundations.

children.heading: Platform
children.text: An elevated flat structure meant to support the weight of people at or above the plane of the ground.

children.heading: Nonconforming Conditions
children.text: Any use, structure, building lot, site characteristics, or sign that was lawfully established prior to the adoption of this Ordinance and has been made nonconforming in result of the adoption of this Ordinance or subsequent amendments, may continue so long as the nonconformity remains otherwise lawful and complies with this section.

children.heading: Primary Building
children.text: See Building, Primary.

children.heading: Primary Entrance
children.text: The main point of access for pedestrians into a building, upper story use, or first floor tenant space.

children.heading: Primary Frontage
children.text: See Frontage, Primary

children.heading: Primary Front Lot Line
children.text: See Lot Line, Primary Front.

children.heading: Primary Front Setback
children.text: See Setback, Primary Front.

children.heading: Primary Ridge Beam
children.text: The highest framing member of a pitched roof to which all rafters attach.

children.heading: Primary Road
children.text: See Road, Primary.

children.heading: Project(ed)
children.text: When a building element extends perpendicular and away from the building face to which it is attached.

children.heading: Property
children.text: Any land, building, or other structure, or part thereof.

children.heading: Public Realm
children.text: All public or civic lands including roads, sidewalks, rights-of-way, and frontage zones.

children.heading: Rafter
children.text: One of several internal beams extending from the eaves to the peak of the roof and constituting its frame.

children.heading: Rear Lot Line
children.text: See Lot Line, Rear.

children.heading: Rear Setback
children.text: The horizontal distance from a rear lot line to the location of structures or use on a lot, measured perpendicularly from the lot line. This area must be maintained clear of permanent structures with the exception of permitted encroachments. See Setback, Rear.

children.heading: Regional
children.text: Uses catering to patrons originating from locations both within the local municipality and elsewhere in the broader area.

children.heading: Residential
children.text: Use characterizing premises available for long-term human dwelling. All residential uses, definitions, and standards may be found in Article 4 Use Standards.

children.heading: Residential Accessory Building
children.text: A building occupied by a use that supports or compliments a residential use, not a commercial use.

children.heading: Retail
children.text: Use characterizing premises available for the sale of merchandise and food service. All retail uses, definitions, and standards may be found in Article 4 Use Standards.

children.heading: Retaining Wall
children.text: A wall that holds the earth at one side at a higher elevation than the earth on the other side.

children.heading: Rezoning
children.text: An amendment to the Official District Map.

children.heading: Right-of-Way
children.text: The total width of any land reserved or dedicated as a road, alley, pedestrian or bicycle way, railway, waterway, or utility line.

children.heading: Ridge Beam
children.text: See Primary Ridge Beam.

children.heading: Road
children.text: A route, track, or way consisting of a bed of exposed mineral soil, gravel, asphalt, or other surfacing material constructed for use by vehicular, pedestrian, and bicycle traffic, and which may have stormwater management facilities, shade trees, and utilities along its borders.

children.heading: Road, Primary
children.text: In determining the Primary Road for Corner lots, Through lots, or any lot that abuts more than one road, the primary road is designated by one or more of the following conditions: • The road that existed first. • The widest road. • The road that carries the greatest amount of traffic. When a lot fronts on more than one road, and multiple roads meet the above criteria, all such roads shall be treated as primary roads.

children.heading: Road, Secondary Road, Private Road, Public
children.text: In determining the Secondary Road for Corner lots, Through lots, or any lot that abuts more than one road, the secondary road or roads are the roads determined not to be the primary road. See Newcastle Road Ordinance. See Newcastle Road Ordinance.

children.heading: Roof Line
children.text: The highest point on any building or structure where an exterior wall or parapet wall encloses roof or floor area, including floor area provided for housing mechanical equipment.

children.heading: ROW
children.text: See Right-of-Way

children.heading: Screen
children.text: A physical barrier between uses, buildings, or activities on adjacent lots or on lots adjacent to a public way, that may be comprised of vegetation, or man-made elements.

children.heading: Shed
children.text: An enclosed, non-insulated building intended for storage.

children.heading: Secondary Frontage
children.text: See Frontage, Secondary.

children.heading: Secondary Front Lot Line
children.text: See Lot Line, Secondary Front.

children.heading: Secondary Front Setback
children.text: See Setback, Secondary Front.

children.heading: Service
children.text: Service uses include any enterprise that provides work performed in an expert manner by an individual or team for the benefit of its customers. The typical service business provides intangible products. Auto-oriented service uses are listed under a separate use category. All service uses, definitions, and standards may be found in Article 6 Use Standards.

children.heading: Setback
children.text: The horizontal distance required between the closest exterior wall of a building or parking and a specified element, such as a lot line, easement, or water body, measured along a perpendicular angle at ground height regardless of natural contours of the land. This area must be maintained clear of permanent structures with the exception of allowed encroachments.

children.heading: Setback, Primary Front
children.text: The distance from a primary lot line bordering a primary road maintained clear from buildings with the exception of encroachments.

children.heading: Setback, Secondary Front
children.text: The distance from a secondary lot line, bordering a secondary road, maintained clear from buildings with the exception of encroachments.

children.heading: Setback, Side
children.text: The distance from a side lot line, maintained clear from buildings with the exception of encroachments.

children.heading: Setback, Rear
children.text: The distance from a rear lot line, maintained clear from buildings with the exception of encroachments.

children.heading: Shade Tree
children.text: Any tree grown specifically for its shade, specifically large trees with spreading canopies.

children.heading: Shopfront
children.text: A first floor building facade, where substantial glazing is required, and the building entrance is located at the grade of the sidewalk or adjacent walkway.

children.heading: Side Lot Line
children.text: See Lot Line, Side.

children.heading: Side Setback
children.text: See Setback, Side.

children.heading: Sidewalk
children.text: The paved section of a right-of-way dedicated exclusively to pedestrian activity.

children.heading: Sign Single Unit Commercial Building Single Unit Residential Building
children.text: Any permanent or temporary name, identification, description, emblem, logo, structure, or device, that is illuminated or non- illuminated; visible or intended to be visible from any public place; and directs attention to a person, product, place, activity, institution, business, organization, activity, or service including any letter, numeral, character, figure, emblem, painting, illustration, banner, pennant, placard, or temporary sign designed to advertise, identify, solicit, or convey information. Signs include devices designed to attract the eye by intermittent or repeated motion and any permanently installed or situated merchandise, including any banner, pennant, placard, or temporary sign, with the exception of window displays. A building occupied soley by a commercial use and no other. A building occupied solely by one residential unit and no other.

children.heading: Site
children.text: A lot or parcel occupied or planned for occupation by a use, including structures and other improvements to the land.

children.heading: Slope
children.text: The ratio of vertical to horizontal distance.

children.heading: Small Animals
children.text: Small domestic animals including rabbits, chickens, goats, ducks, alpaca, emu, and other similarly sized animals raised for home use or for profit.

children.heading: Solar Farm
children.text: A site at which photovoltaic modules are used to generate and produce electric power for distribution to consumers, typically managed by a single entity.

children.heading: Soffit
children.text: The flat underside of an overhanging building element such as eaves or cornices.

children.heading: Special District
children.text: An area that due to its intrinsic size, arrangement of buildings, or other unique characteristics cannot meet the standards of an existing core district and is therefore established as a discrete district with a customized set of standards, building standards, and site standards.

children.heading: Special Requirements
children.text: Designations on the Town of Newcastle Official Zoning Map that indicate additional standards.

children.heading: Story
children.text: An occupiable floor of a building as distinct from the area contained under the pitch of a roof or a basement.

children.heading: Street Tree
children.text: A tree planted within the furnishing zone as an element of a road.

children.heading: Streetwall
children.text: A condition where buildings, through their consistent arrangement along a street, create the impression of forming a wall. While the buildings can be separated, a streetwall is predicated on the buildings all having a similar front setback that is in close proximity to the street or civic space.

children.heading: Streetwall, Continuous
children.text: A streetwall condition comprised by buildings that are predominantly attached on the sides and that all have a consistent front setback directly on the property line.

children.heading: Structure
children.text: Anything constructed or erected, the use of which requires more or less permanent location on the ground, or attached to something having permanent location on the ground.

children.heading: Substantial Modification
children.text: Alteration of a primary building in such a way as to cause an expansion in the footprint of the main building mass.

children.heading: Swale
children.text: A low or slightly depressed natural area for drainage.

children.heading: Swimming Pool
children.text: Any structure that is intended for recreational bathing or swimming that contains water deeper than 24 inches. This includes in-ground swimming pools, above-ground or on-ground pools, hot tub, spa, and inflatable pools.

children.heading: Terraced
children.text: An area of sloped land that has been made into a series of level areas, resembling steps.

children.heading: Through Lot
children.text: A building lot that has two or more frontages along one or more non-intersecting private or public roads.

children.heading: Top Plate
children.text: The topmost horizontal, load-bearing member in a framed wall system.

children.heading: Tree Pit
children.text: A hole filled with soil for the planting and growth of a street tree. Tree pits have surface area open to air and water flow.

children.heading: Tree, Shade
children.text: See Shade Tree.

children.heading: Tree Shape
children.text: Refers to 6 unique categories of trees, defined by a unique shape and used as a way to regulate trees along roads or within or civic space.

children.heading: Tree Plantings
children.text: The required numbers of trees that must be planted per square foot of ground.

children.heading: Unit
children.text: A single, internally connected space that comprises a building or a part of a building that can be occupied by any one of the use categories included in Article 4 Use Standards. (See Dwelling Unit and Non-dwelling Unit).

children.heading: Unit Floor Area
children.text: The net Floor Area of any single Residential or Non-Residential unit. [See Floor Area, Net (Unit)]

children.heading: Upper Story
children.text: Syn: Upper Floor

children.heading: Use
children.text: Any actual or intended occupation, business, operation, function, or activity carried out on a lot, within a structure, or within part of a structure.

children.heading: Use, Temporary
children.text: A use established for a fixed period of time with the intent to discontinue such use upon expiration of the time period.

children.heading: Use Category
children.text: A group of uses collapsed into a category of similar types for the purpose of simplifying the regulation of uses.

children.heading: Utility Equipment
children.text: Utility equipment includes vents, exhaust, and utility boxes.

children.heading: Variance
children.text: A departure from the strict terms or expressed standards of this Code, where such departure is authorized in accordance with Section 10 of Chapter 40A of the Maine General Laws.

children.heading: Vertical Plane
children.text: A flat surface perpendicular to the ground or horizontal plane.

children.heading: Waiver
children.text: A predetermined type of deviation, within specific limitations, from the block, lot, and/or road standards of a specific district in this Code.

children.heading: Wall
children.text: A low structure typically built of masonry that defines an area or a boundary.

children.heading: Waterfront Lot
children.text: A building lot that has frontage along a body of water and frontage along a private or public road.

children.heading: Width
children.text: In a three-dimensional measurement system, width is a horizontal measurement, distinct and shorter than length.

children.heading: Wind Farm
children.text: A group of wind turbines in the same location used to produce electricity.

children.heading: Windows & Doors
children.text: The arrangement, proportioning, and design of openings on every exterior wall of a building, including windows and doors but excluding entrances and doors for parking, loading, and service facilities. If a garage door is more than 50% glass, it is counted as a window and door.

children.heading: Windows & Doors, Ground Story
children.text: The percentage of openings present on a building’s ground floor.

children.heading: Windows & Doors, Upper Story
children.text: The percentage of openings on the upper stories, each considered independently.

children.heading: Worker
children.text: Workers include all people engaged in labor and who are either full- time, part-time, temporary, contract, or self-employed.

children.heading: Yard
children.text: A privately-owned area that is adjacent to a building and often times described in relation to the building, such as front yard, side yard, or rear yard.

children.heading: Zoning Permit
children.text: An approval that certifies that a project complies with all applicable municipal ordinances.
